client: I've been really struggling at work lately, and honestly I wasn't sure if coming here would even do anything. There's this colleague of mine, Jessica, who keeps presenting my ideas in meetings like they're her own, and my manager doesn't seem to notice or care. It's making me feel completely invisible, like nothing I do actually matters, and I'm starting to worry that my job might even be at risk if I can't find a way to stand out.
therapist: What you're describing sounds genuinely painful — having your contributions overlooked or taken credit for can deeply shake your sense of worth and security at work. I also notice you came in with some doubt about whether this would even help, and I want you to know that sharing something this difficult is already a meaningful step. I'm curious — when you imagine feeling truly *seen* at work, what would that look like for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, when I imagine feeling truly seen at work, it would just mean someone acknowledging that an idea came from me — like, even a small "hey, good thinking" directed at me specifically, not watching my manager present my work as his own in a meeting. But even as I say that out loud, I feel kind of embarrassed, like maybe I'm being too needy or making too big a deal out of something that happens to everyone. I guess part of me wonders if feeling seen is even realistic to expect in a workplace, or if I'm just setting myself up to be disappointed again.
therapist: What you're describing — wanting acknowledgment for your own contributions — isn't neediness, it's a completely human and reasonable need, and it's worth noticing how quickly you moved to dismiss it as "too much." That self-critical voice that calls your needs excessive is worth paying attention to, because it might be getting in the way of you advocating for yourself. What do you think that voice is trying to protect you from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I mean... I guess when I think about it, that voice is probably trying to protect me from being rejected or looking pathetic. Like if I never ask for recognition, I can't be told I don't deserve it. But honestly, hearing you say it that way makes me feel kind of sad, because it means I've been preemptively shutting myself down before anyone else even gets the chance to.
therapist: That insight — recognizing that you've been your own first rejection — takes real courage to sit with, and the sadness you're feeling makes complete sense. There's something tender in your voice as you say it, like you're grieving a little for all the times you silenced yourself before anyone else could. I'm wondering, if that protective voice weren't quite so loud, what's one small thing you might have done differently — maybe even recently at work?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I sit with that for a moment, and yeah, it does feel like grief, actually. Like I've been carrying around this really efficient rejection machine inside me, and it got so good at its job that I stopped even noticing it was running. If it weren't so loud... I think maybe I would have spoken up in that meeting last Tuesday when I had an idea, instead of just writing it down in my notebook and never saying anything.
therapist: "Rejection machine" is such a vivid and honest way to put it, and the fact that you can name it so clearly now suggests you're already starting to step outside of it. That moment last Tuesday — the idea sitting in your notebook instead of in the room — feels like an important one to hold onto, not with self-criticism, but as a kind of evidence of what becomes possible when that voice quiets down. What do you think it would have taken, in that moment, to say it out loud?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think what it would have taken is just... not caring so much about what everyone in the room would think. But that's the thing — I do care, a lot, and I can't just switch that off. Even imagining saying it out loud right now makes my chest feel tight, like I'm already bracing for the moment someone looks at me like the idea was stupid.
therapist: That tightness in your chest is really important information — your body is already rehearsing the rejection before anything has even happened, which is such a telling sign of how long this pattern has been running. You're right that you can't just switch off caring, and honestly, we wouldn't want to — caring means these things matter to you, and that's not a flaw. I'm curious, though: when you imagine that moment and someone *doesn't* look at you like the idea was stupid, what happens in your body then?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That's a weird question to sit with, because honestly my first instinct was to say nothing changes, like I just assumed the good outcome wouldn't happen. But when I actually try to imagine someone nodding, looking interested, taking my idea seriously... there's this tiny flicker of something, almost like relief, but it disappears really fast because my brain immediately goes "okay but that's just one person, it won't last." It's like I can't let myself stay in that good feeling for more than a second before I'm already bracing for it to fall apart.
therapist: That "tiny flicker" you described is actually really significant — it means part of you *can* receive good things, even if another part rushes in almost immediately to take them away. It's like you've built an eviction notice for positive experiences before they even get comfortable. I'm wondering if we could slow that moment down together — what would it mean about you, and about the world, if that good feeling were actually allowed to stay?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I like that image you used — the eviction notice — because yeah, that's exactly what it feels like, like I can't even let something good settle before I'm already kicking it out. But if I'm honest, I think letting it stay feels dangerous, like if I actually believe I deserve good things and then they disappear, that's so much worse than just never trusting them in the first place. It's almost like staying lonely and guarded is... safer, even though I know how miserable it makes me.
therapist: What you just named is one of the most honest and painful paradoxes a person can carry — choosing a smaller, safer life to avoid the risk of a bigger loss. The way you said it, quickly and almost matter-of-factly, makes me wonder if part of you has had to make peace with that trade-off for a long time, even while another part of you is sitting here today, which tells me you haven't fully accepted it. What do you think brought you to the point where that bargain started to feel less worth it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think what you said about "not fully accepting it" kind of hit me harder than I expected, because I've been telling myself for years that I made peace with it. But lately it's like the walls of that smaller life are closing in, and the loneliness just feels louder than the safety does. I guess what brought me here is that I started to realize I'm not actually protected from pain by keeping people at a distance — I'm just... sitting in a different kind of pain, alone with it.
therapist: What you just said — that you're not avoiding pain, just sitting in a different kind of it, alone — is a profound and brave realization, and it sounds like it's landing in your body even as you say it. There's something quietly significant about the way you're holding this, like it's both a relief to name and a little overwhelming to fully take in. I want to stay with this for a moment — what feels different now, having said that out loud, compared to when it was just a thought you carried by yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: It's strange, because saying it out loud made it feel more real, but also somehow less suffocating, like I'd been holding my breath without knowing it. I think when it was just in my head, it felt like a shameful secret, like there was something wrong with me for choosing to be alone rather than stay in that relationship. But hearing myself say it, and you not reacting like it's a terrible thing, makes me wonder if maybe I've been judging myself way harder than I needed to.
therapist: That image of finally exhaling after holding your breath without knowing it is beautiful, and it makes so much sense that naming something out loud in a safe space can loosen its grip. What strikes me is how you've been carrying a verdict about yourself — that choosing to leave was shameful — without ever really putting it on trial to see if it holds up. I'm curious: now that you're starting to question that harsh judgment, what do you think a fairer, more compassionate version of that story might sound like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess a fairer version would be something like... I left because I was drowning, and staying would have made things worse for both of us. But even as I say that out loud, there's this voice in the back of my head that jumps in and says "that's just an excuse you're telling yourself to feel better." I don't know how to trust the kinder version of the story when the harsher one feels so much more... real, somehow.
therapist: It's worth pausing on something you just said — that the harsher story feels more *real*, because I think that's actually a clue about how long you've been living inside it, not evidence that it's true. The kinder version isn't an excuse; it's just newer and less worn-in, like a path you haven't walked enough times yet for it to feel familiar. I'm wondering — whose voice does that critical one sound like, the one that calls the compassionate story "just an excuse"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
